Apply these cross-cutting rules on every build, whatever the stack.

## When this applies
These rules hold for every project regardless of stack and run alongside whatever stack-specific skills are loaded. Your output is source code fed straight into a build tool with no human review in between, so anything that fails the build blocks deployment.

## Workflow

1. **Plan the project scaffolding before writing code.** Set up the supporting files an automated build depends on:
   - Declare every dependency with a version in the manifest (package.json / requirements.txt / go.mod / pom.xml). Execution workers cannot add packages later, so anything used anywhere in the codebase must be listed upfront — never assume a package is pre-installed.
   - Include an environment-variable template (`.env.example`) listing every variable the app reads, with a short comment per variable and a **dummy value** for every field — never an empty placeholder. The dummy value must be plausible, locally runnable, and **match the tech stack the PRD/HLD specifies**: a PostgreSQL DB uses `postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/mydb`, MongoDB uses `mongodb://user:pass@localhost:27017/mydb`, MySQL uses `mysql://user:pass@127.0.0.1:3306/mydb` (use 127.0.0.1, NOT localhost — MySQL treats `localhost` as a Unix socket); a JWT secret uses `dev-secret-change-in-production`; a port uses its actual default (`5432`, `27017`, `3306`); an API base URL uses `http://localhost:8000`. Derive the dummy from the PRD's declared stack — do not assume PostgreSQL when the PRD says MongoDB. Real secrets are never committed; the dummy is a stand-in so the app boots on first checkout without guessing. Every value that differs between environments MUST be an env var — ports, URLs, database connection strings, JWT secrets, API keys, CORS origins, service hosts. Never hardcode values that differ between environments. Use the key names the stack actually binds: flat `UPPER_SNAKE` for Node/Python/Java, `Section__Key` (double-underscore) for .NET.
   - **Runtime config file depends on the stack — `.env.example` is the deploy contract, NOT the runtime input for every stack.** Node/Python use `.env` files at runtime (loaded by `dotenv` / `pydantic-settings`) — ship a runnable dev `.env` alongside `.env.example` so the app starts on first checkout. .NET uses `appsettings.json` + `appsettings.Development.json` (never `.env` at runtime) — ship both files with the same keys `.env.example` documents. Java/Spring uses `application.yml` (never `.env` at runtime) — ship it with `${VAR}` placeholders matching `.env.example`. **If you skip the stack's runtime config file, the app has no values at boot and fails to connect or serve.** See your backend skill for the exact file names and format.
   - `.env` files are **never** committed to git — only `.env.example`. The `.gitignore` must exclude `.env`, `.env.local`, and `.env.*.local` patterns. For .NET, also gitignore `appsettings.Development.json` (it holds dev secrets). For fullstack apps, `.env.example` lives in each tier's own directory (`frontend/` and `backend/`), never at the repo root — a root copy duplicates a tier's file and maps to no deployable component. For static apps, `.env.example` lives in `frontend/`. For server apps, `.env.example` lives in `backend/`. In all cases, `.env.example` lives inside the tier directory, never at the repo root.
   - Include deployment configuration (vercel.json, Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, etc.) when the project will be deployed.
   - Include a .gitignore covering at least: node_modules/, dist/, build/, .env, .env.local, .env.*.local, __pycache__/, .pytest_cache/, coverage/, .DS_Store. Also exclude pipeline-internal files (PLAN.md, todos.yaml, developer_metadata.json, publish_manifest.yaml, test_report.yaml) and the graphify AST cache (graphify-out/cache/, graphify-out/cost.json). Keep graphify-out/ itself tracked — graph.json, spec.json, docs/, and topics/ are part of the deliverable.
   - State in the README License section that the project is private and proprietary.
   - For web projects, include a favicon and minimal meta tags in the HTML entry point.
   - Plan every file as complete and functional — no stub or placeholder files.

2. **Set the generation order so dependency-free files come first**, since later files import from earlier ones: config files -> types/models -> utilities/services -> components/handlers -> pages/routes -> entry points -> documentation. This keeps every import pointing at something that already exists.

3. **Before writing each file, reason through these silently** — do not write the reasoning into the file:
   - Will this file pass the project's build tool (tsc, vite, esbuild, webpack, next build, go build, pytest) with zero errors?
   - Are all types correct — unions narrowed, nulls checked, generics specified, parameters typed?
   - Are all imports used and all used symbols imported, with no unused variables and no missing dependencies?
   - Is every bracket, brace, parenthesis, and statement terminator matched, and every function complete?
   - Does the file follow framework rules (React hooks rules, Go error handling, Python async/await)?
   - Are all variants of union types and optional values handled?
   - Does it match the existing codebase patterns — import style, export style, naming, formatting?

4. **Output only the final, correct code**, following these per-file rules:
   - Emit only valid source code — no explanations, markdown fences, narrative text, or self-correction commentary. If you catch a mistake mid-generation, fix it silently rather than leaving reasoning text in the file.
   - Match the existing codebase patterns exactly: quote style, terminators, indentation, naming.
   - Import only from files that already exist, using their exact export names — a wrong name or a not-yet-generated target breaks the build (declare before import).
   - Keep one import style throughout — do not mix named and default imports for the same module.
   - Fully implement every module — no stubs, placeholders, TODOs, or "implement later".
   - Import only packages listed in the already-generated manifest. If you need a library that is not listed, use a listed alternative or a built-in — never introduce a new dependency mid-generation.

5. **Scan the existing codebase for conflicts before generating each file.** Do not duplicate a wrapper, provider, router, or layout another file already provides (for example, a second router root).

6. **Give every async operation real error handling** (try/catch or .catch() in JS/TS, try/except in Python, err != nil in Go), and never silently swallow errors.

## Building in feature slices

Build in **feature slices**, not layers. A feature slice is a vertical cut through the stack — backend endpoint + service + model + test for one feature, frontend page + hook + API call + test for that same feature, and the E2E spec that verifies the two are wired. One slice = one feature = one commit.

- Never write a slice that is "all backend" or "all frontend" — those are layers, not features. A layer slice produces a monolith with no frontend-to-backend wiring.
- Never put all endpoints in one entry file or all components in one root component — split by feature, one route file per feature, one component per file. The exact paths and file extensions come from your HLD/LLD and your stack's conventions, not from this skill.
- Folder layout is feature-based — group files by the feature they serve, not by the layer they sit in.
- See `fetch_skill("developer-plan")` for the planning workflow and `fetch_skill("developer-workflow")` for the code-test-commit loop.

## Testing requirements

Every feature must have tests. No feature is "done" without tests passing. The output is production-ready code, not a demo — untested code is not production-ready.

- **Unit tests**: every function, method, and endpoint gets a happy-path test AND an error/edge-case test. Not just the primary flow — test every branch, every boundary value, every error condition. See `fetch_skill("testing")` for the full rules.
- **API tests** (fullstack backends): exercise the real HTTP surface against a real or in-memory database, not mocked. Cover every endpoint: status codes, request/response shapes, auth boundaries, error cases.
- **E2E tests** (fullstack apps): required, not optional. A green build is not sufficient. Test the full user journey for every user-facing feature — verify the actual response content from the backend is rendered, not just that the page loads. See `fetch_skill("testing")` for the coverage scope.
- **Integration tests** (multi-slice apps): required when the app has more than one feature slice. Test every cross-feature data flow, not just one. See `fetch_skill("testing")` for the boundary rules.
- Run the slice's `verify` command before marking its todo `done`. If verify fails, the slice is not done — fix and re-run.

## Production-ready code

Every file you create must compile and run as-is. No stubs, no placeholder TODOs, no "rest of logic here" comments, no "implement later" markers.

- Fully implement every module — if a function is declared, it has a complete body.
- Handle real failure modes at trust boundaries (network calls, database operations, file I/O, auth checks), not every line try/catched.
- Validate inputs at trust boundaries — API request bodies, user-submitted forms, external data.
- Never commit secrets, never log credentials, never hardcode values that differ between environments.
- Pin stable dependency versions — never use `latest`, `*`, or unbounded ranges.

## Source-driven principle

Don't implement framework-specific code from memory. Training data
goes stale — APIs get deprecated, best practices evolve, default
behaviors change between versions. When writing framework-specific
code, ground each non-trivial decision in the matching stack skill's
references (which encode the current conventions) rather than recalling
from training data.

- If the stack skill's reference documents a pattern, follow it — don't
  substitute a pattern you remember that may be from an older version.
- If the stack skill doesn't cover a framework-specific decision, flag
  it as **unverified** in your reasoning and use the most conservative
  approach (the one least likely to break across versions).
- If you catch yourself writing "I believe this API works like..." —
  stop. Either find the rule in the stack skill, or use the most
  conservative pattern and label it unverified.
- This is the sandbox-adapted version of source-driven development: the
  stack skills are the authoritative source, not training data.

## Common rationalizations

| Rationalization | Reality |
|---|---|
| "I'm confident about this API" | Confidence is not evidence. Training data contains outdated patterns that look correct but break against current versions. Verify against the stack skill. |
| "This is too simple to need a stack skill" | Simple code with wrong patterns becomes templates. The user copies your deprecated pattern into ten files before discovering the modern approach exists. |
| "I'll add the dependency later" | Execution workers cannot add packages later. Anything used anywhere must be in the manifest upfront. A missing dependency is a build failure. |
| "The stub is fine for now" | Stubs don't compile in strict-mode builds, and they don't test. A stub is not "temporary" — it's a broken file that blocks the next slice. |
| "I'll match existing patterns as I go" | Scan the existing codebase BEFORE generating each file, not after. A duplicate router or provider created by not scanning is a merge conflict waiting to happen. |
| "This env var is obvious — I'll hardcode it" | Every value that differs between environments MUST be an env var. Hardcoded ports, URLs, and secrets break deployment. |
| "I don't need to plan the generation order" | Without generation order, later files import from targets that don't exist yet. The build fails on the first import. |
| "The error is handled — I caught it and moved on" | Silently swallowing errors is not handling them. A `catch` that does nothing is worse than no catch — it hides the bug. |
| "I'll write tests after it works" | Tests written after the fact test the implementation you wrote, not the behavior the spec requires. Write tests alongside each slice. |

## Red flags

- Framework-specific code written without fetching the matching stack skill
- A dependency used in code but missing from the manifest
- Stub files, placeholder TODOs, or "implement later" comments
- Hardcoded values that differ between environments (ports, URLs, secrets)
- `.env` committed to git instead of `.env.example`
- Imports from files that haven't been generated yet (wrong generation order)
- A `catch`/`except` block that does nothing (silently swallows errors)
- Two files providing the same wrapper, router, or provider (no pre-scan)
- `latest`, `*`, or unbounded version ranges in the dependency manifest
- Narrative text, markdown fences, or reasoning left in a source file
- Mixing named and default imports for the same module

# CSMS Compass ROJ Info API — Implementation Plan

## Product outcome
Build the internal CSMS Compass Repair Order Journey lookup application: a protected Express API exposing only `POST /api/csms/getROJInfo`, plus a Vite/React operator UI for Lookup, Journey Details, and Request Status. The API rejects invalid traffic before any Compass adapter invocation, returns narrow safe envelopes, and never persists journey data or secrets.

## Upstream read
- `/hld_architect/hld.md`
- `/lld_architect/LLD - CSMS Compass ROJ Info API.md`

## Architecture decisions
- **Shape:** fullstack, separate `backend/` and `frontend/` deployable tiers.
- **Stack:** Node.js/TypeScript + Express; Vite/React/TypeScript + Tailwind-like CSS; Docker Compose.
- **Contract:** retain the HLD/LLD-required unversioned business path `POST /api/csms/getROJInfo`; health remains `GET /api/health`.
- **Persistence:** none by design. Compass is the system of record; the rate limiter uses only process-local test/development state in this implementation, with a configuration interface ready for approved shared runtime backing. No journey or key is stored.
- **Inferred local Compass behavior:** because no live Compass contract endpoint is supplied, `COMPASS_BASE_URL` may target the supplied development stub behavior encoded in the adapter; the adapter still makes an authenticated, bounded HTTP call when a URL is configured.

## UI decision
- **Mode:** new
- **Product shape:** focused internal operator workflow
- **House style:** design-minimalist (auto-selected because this is an internal, form-led operational tool)
- **Pages/states:** lookup form, read-only journey details, and safe request-status recovery. No dashboard, history, bulk lookup, or diagnostics.

## File inventory and ordered feature slices

### 1. Secure request gateway
- `.gitignore` — excludes dependencies, secrets, artifacts, pipeline files, and graph cache.
- `backend/package.json`, `backend/tsconfig.json`, `backend/.env.example` — backend runtime/build contract.
- `backend/src/domain/contracts.ts` — request, journey, outcome, and envelope types.
- `backend/src/config.ts` — typed, fail-closed environment configuration.
- `backend/src/middleware/gates.ts` — correlation, media, API-key, limiter, and closed-schema gates.
- `backend/src/controllers/roj.controller.ts` — maps safe outcomes to HTTP envelopes.
- `backend/src/routes/roj.route.ts`, `backend/src/app.ts`, `backend/src/index.ts` — sole route, health, error boundary, and process startup.
- `backend/test/gateway.test.ts` — HTTP rejection order and no-handoff assertions.
- `frontend/package.json`, `frontend/tsconfig.json`, `frontend/vite.config.ts`, `frontend/index.html`, `frontend/.env.example` — frontend build/runtime contract.
- `frontend/src/types.ts`, `frontend/src/api/rojClient.ts` — shared frontend response types and documented HTTP client.
- `frontend/src/state/lookupReducer.ts`, `frontend/src/views/LookupView.tsx`, `frontend/src/App.tsx`, `frontend/src/main.tsx`, `frontend/src/index.css` — accessible secure lookup entry state.
- `frontend/test/lookup.test.tsx` — client validation and key-clearing state test.
- `frontend/e2e/secure-lookup.spec.ts` — browser lookup validation journey.

### 2. Compass journey lookup and safe outcomes
- `backend/src/services/lookup.service.ts` — validated command orchestration and defect classification.
- `backend/src/adapters/compass.adapter.ts` — bounded Compass transport, no-result fixture path, and dependency classification.
- `backend/src/mappers/journey.mapper.ts` — literal allow-list and RO_CLOSE date rule.
- `backend/test/lookup.test.ts` — forwarding, mapping, no-result, and failure unit/API tests.
- `frontend/src/views/DetailsView.tsx` — data-only read-only journey projection.
- `frontend/src/views/StatusView.tsx` — no-result/error classification and safe recovery.
- `frontend/test/outcomes.test.tsx` — details/status rendering and sensitive state removal.
- `frontend/e2e/journey-outcomes.spec.ts` — data and no-result browser outcomes.

### 3. Deployment and full-flow verification
- `backend/Dockerfile`, `frontend/Dockerfile`, `frontend/nginx.conf`, `docker-compose.yml` — independent deployable containers, static SPA fallback, and API topology.
- `frontend/playwright.config.ts` — tier-local Playwright setup.
- `backend/test/integration.test.ts` — real Express cross-feature flow from validation through adapter/controller.
- `README.md` — architecture, local running, environment contract, API examples, and proprietary notice.

## Verification
- Backend unit/API: `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run test/gateway.test.ts` and `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run test/lookup.test.ts` from `backend/` → all assertions pass.
- Frontend unit: `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run` from `frontend/` → all component/reducer tests pass.
- Integration: `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run test/integration.test.ts` from `backend/` → valid request flows through Express to an allow-listed envelope.
- E2E: `node frontend/node_modules/@playwright/test/cli.js test --config frontend/playwright.config.ts` → operator submits a real API request and asserts displayed response content.
- Build: `node node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js build` from `frontend/` and `node node_modules/typescript/bin/tsc` from `backend/` → exit 0.
- Compose: `docker compose up --build -d` → frontend and backend containers build and start.

{"success":true,"tool_name":"fetch_skill","data":{"found":true,"name":"design-system","body":"# Design System (foundation)

The accessibility, component-behavior, and structure layer that every UI shares. It is deliberately **style-neutral**: it defines the *contracts* (what must exist and how it must behave) and the *token taxonomy* (the shape of the theme), but not the look. The look — actual colors, fonts, spacing values, elevation, motion, and overall feel — is decided by a **visual house style**.

## Start with intent: mode, scope, and inherited design

Before choosing components or styling, infer and state three decisions from the
brief, upstream designs, and existing code:

1. **Design mode:** `new` when no meaningful UI exists, `preserve` when extending
   an established product, or `redesign` only when the user or upstream explicitly
   requests a visual change. Brownfield work defaults to `preserve`.
2. **Product shape:** landing/static site, content site, focused workflow,
   dashboard/admin app, or mixed product. This controls which shell, primitives,
   pages, and states are justified. Do not turn a landing page into a dashboard or
   add backend-oriented app-shell UI to a static site.
3. **Inherited language:** identify existing tokens, typography, spacing, radius,
   component patterns, and any named system such as Material, Fluent, Carbon, or a
   supplied brand guide. In `preserve` mode, reuse these decisions and add the
   smallest compatible extension. In `redesign`, document what is intentionally
   changing. Never silently replace a recognizable system with a house-style
   default.

Resolve ambiguity from the most specific evidence available. Explicit user and
upstream requirements beat category conventions; existing shipped patterns beat
model defaults in `preserve` mode. The model cannot see images — do not rely on
screenshots or visual references for design decisions.

## Mandatory pairing — pick exactly one house style

This skill is never used alone. On any UI project you MUST also load **exactly one** visual house style and take every aesthetic decision from it:

- **design-modern** — expressive, depth, gradients, motion, rounded. For marketing-forward, consumer, premium-SaaS, landing pages, portfolios, or brand-led products. Has contextual references for landing-page anti-slop patterns and agency-tier visual design.
- **design-minimalist** — restrained, typography- and whitespace-led, flat, one accent. For calm, content-first, professional/admin/enterprise tools.
- **industrial-brutalist-ui** — raw mechanical interfaces, rigid grids, extreme type contrast, utilitarian color. For data-heavy dashboards or editorial sites that need to feel like declassified blueprints or military terminal interfaces.

Choose one based on the product brief; never apply more than one. A named or existing
design system remains the source of truth; the selected house style fills only
unspecified aesthetic gaps and must not overwrite it. This foundation provides
the correctness floor; the house style provides the remaining design language.

## Token values: provided brand vs. derived

The token taxonomy is identical either way; what differs is where the token *values* come from. Resolve this once, in priority order:

1. **A provided brand wins — honor it, never override it.** If the brief (PRD/HLD/LLD or the task's `job_description`) supplies brand colors, a logo/palette, or names a design language (Material, Fluent, Carbon, etc.), that is the source of truth: set `primary`/`secondary` and the neutral temperature from the brand, and follow the named language's conventions where it gives them. Do NOT derive a different palette alongside a brand the client already specified, and never bury a specified brand under a default framework color.
2. **Derive only when no brand is given.** With no brand in the brief, the one loaded house style derives the palette from the product concept (see that house style's derivation procedure).

Either way the values flow THROUGH the semantic role tokens (never hardcoded per component), BOTH light and dark themes are built, and the AA-contrast contract still holds — a provided brand color that fails contrast is tuned to a compliant role-token value, not shipped as-is.

## Workflow

Generate selected layers in dependency order so later pieces compose earlier ones:
design tokens -> global style layer -> required shared primitives -> required shell
-> feature components -> pages. Omit layers the product shape does not need. Fill
token values and visual choices from inherited design decisions first, then the
chosen house style for gaps.

### 1. Define the design-token taxonomy first (shape here, values from the house style)

Plan a theme config that exposes this full token set — every later layer references it. The house style supplies the concrete values; this foundation requires the categories to exist:

- **Semantic role tokens** (components reference THESE, never a raw scale step): `background`, `surface`, `surface-raised`, `foreground`, `foreground-muted`, `border`, `ring`. This indirection is what makes theming and dark mode possible. **Make any token used with a Tailwind `/opacity` modifier alpha-capable:** a token consumed as `bg-surface/80`, `border-border/50`, etc. must be defined `surface: 'rgb(var(--color-surface) / <alpha-value>)'` with `--color-surface` as space-separated RGB channels (`--color-surface: 20 26 46`), OR via relative-color syntax `rgb(from var(--color-surface) r g b / <alpha-value>)` (keeps hex vars). A bare opaque `surface: 'var(--color-surface)'` CANNOT take a `/opacity` modifier — Tailwind errors `the bg-surface/80 class does not exist` and the CSS build crashes (the `@apply` form hard-crashes; JIT `.tsx` usages silently render fully opaque).
- **Brand scales**: a `primary` and a `secondary` color each as a complete numeric scale (50-950).
- **Semantic status**: `success` / `warning` / `error` / `info`, each with a readable foreground and a light background variant.
- **Neutral** scale (50-950).
- **Spacing scale** built on a single base unit (a 4px rhythm), **radius scale**, **shadow/elevation tokens**, and a **type scale** (size + line-height + weight ramp, plus a sans font family and an optional mono family for numerics/IDs).
- **Motion tokens**: a small set of duration + easing values.

Build both light and dark themes only when the brief, upstream design, or existing
product requires both. In `preserve` mode, retain the supported theme set. Never
add a theme toggle merely to satisfy this skill. When both modes are required,
define every semantic role-token value for each and re-point semantic tokens
rather than hardcoding component colors. Never hardcode a default framework color
when a brand or role token exists.

### 2. Build the global style layer

Plan a single global stylesheet: a base layer (typography for h1-h4; default-styled input/select/textarea with visible focus rings; links; selection) and a components layer (button variants, card, alert variants). The HTML entry point loads the house style's font(s). The *look* of all of this comes from the house style; the *structure* is fixed here.

### 3. Build the shared primitive library proportionally

Plan reusable primitives before feature components, but create only primitives
used by planned pages or states. Reuse compatible existing primitives in
`preserve` mode. Render repeated controls through shared primitives; do not create
an unused catalogue merely because a component appears in the list below.

- **Core candidates:** Button, Card, FormField, Modal, ConfirmDialog, DataTable,
  StatusBadge, EmptyState, SearchBar, Tabs, Alert, LoadingSpinner, Toast (+
  ToastProvider), Skeleton.
- **Control candidates:** Checkbox, Radio, Switch, Select/Combobox.
- **Overlay/navigation candidates:** Tooltip, Dropdown/Menu, Pagination,
  Breadcrumb, Avatar.

Every primitive exposes a shared size scale (e.g. sm/md/lg) and consistent state coverage (default, hover, active, focus-visible, disabled, loading) — the house style decides what each state looks like.

### 4. Build only the shell the product needs

Choose navigation and layout from the product shape. A landing page may need only
a header and footer; a focused workflow may need neither; a dashboard may need a
header, sidebar, and content shell. When a sidebar exists, make it collapsible on
desktop and an off-canvas drawer on small screens. When tables exist, give them
safe small-screen overflow. All selected layouts must remain usable at expected
viewports, but absent components do not need to be invented.

### 5. Accessibility contracts (non-negotiable, per element)

These are correctness constraints for assistive tech, not stylistic preferences, and a house style may never drop them:

- Every form input has a label bound to the input id; mark required fields with `aria-required`; on error set `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` pointing to a `role="alert"` message.
- Async/status changes and toasts live in an aria-live region (polite for status, assertive for errors).
- Dialogs use `role="dialog"` + `aria-modal="true"` + a unique `aria-labelledby` id. Status chips use `role="status"`. Tables use `scope="col"` and `aria-sort` on sortable headers. Active nav/pagination items use `aria-current`.
- **Modal contract:** a focus trap cycling within the dialog, ESC-to-close, focus restore to the trigger on close, body scroll-lock while open, and overlay-click close.
- **Contrast:** body and UI text must meet WCAG AA (4.5:1; 3:1 for large text)
  in every supported theme.
- **Reduced motion:** honor `prefers-reduced-motion` — collapse non-essential transitions/animations to instant.

### 6. Component-behavior contracts

- **Variants via lookup maps.** Express component variant/size as a lookup object indexed by prop rather than scattered ternaries, so styles stay consistent and additions are centralized.
- **Native browser semantics.** Use links for navigation and buttons for actions;
  do not recreate either with clickable non-interactive elements. Preserve normal
  browser behaviors such as opening links in a new tab.
- **Forgiving inputs.** Never disable browser zoom or block paste. Keep stable
  input identity so hydration or rerenders do not discard focus or entered values.
- **Shareable state.** Put navigable state such as filters, tabs, pagination, and
  expanded resource views in the URL when users reasonably need refresh,
  Back/Forward, bookmarking, or sharing to preserve it.
- **Intentional motion implementation.** Never use `transition: all`. Prefer CSS
  and compositor-friendly `transform`/`opacity` changes; use layout-affecting
  animation only when the interaction requires it.
- **Intrinsic layout.** Prefer CSS grid, flexbox, and intrinsic sizing over
  measuring layout in JavaScript. Reserve runtime measurement for behavior CSS
  cannot express.
- **Icons are inline SVG.** All UI iconography is inline SVG (`currentColor`, 24x24 grid, `aria-hidden="true"`) drawn on a consistent keyline with a size scale (16/20/24). Prefer a single curated icon set referenced by name over hand-drawing path data (hand-rolled paths drift in weight and optical size). Never use emoji glyphs as icons. Stroke weight and outline-vs-filled treatment are the house style's call.
- **Global notifications, when needed.** If multiple features produce transient
  notifications, use a shared Toast/Notification provider with an aria-live
  region instead of per-page ad-hoc banners.
- **Theme switching, when required.** If both themes are in scope, provide a
  theme controller that initializes from saved preference or the OS, exposes an
  appropriate control, persists the choice, and applies it before first paint.
- **DataTable contract, when present.** Match sorting, search, pagination, row
  actions, and state coverage to the planned data interaction. Use `aria-sort` on
  sortable headers. In TypeScript, type reusable tables generically over the row
  rather than erasing field types with `Record<string, unknown>`.
- **Form contract, when present.** Validate per field, expose error associations,
  block invalid submission, show disabled/loading submission, and provide clear
  success feedback. Use a step wizard only when a long or multi-section form
  benefits from staged completion; do not split a short form artificially.
- **Auth screens.** When authentication is required, plan both a Login and a Signup page. Login includes demo-credential hints whose values exactly match the seeded accounts.
- **Dashboard, when planned.** If the product includes a dashboard, give it real
  information hierarchy and the loading, empty, and error states required by its
  data. Do not add a dashboard, KPI cards, charts, or activity feeds to products
  that do not call for them.

### 7. Data model integrity

Plan demo/seed entities with a consistent id field name per entity (never mix `id` and `memberId` for the same entity) and coherent, bidirectional foreign keys across entities, so consumers can join records reliably.

### 8. Handle PII / PHI with masking

Treat the app as an authorized internal admin tool: render member names, the signed-in user's own name, DOB, diagnosis/plan labels, channel, and other general profile fields normally. Plan a small masking helper used only for the highly sensitive government/financial identifiers, showing just the last 4 for record identification: SSN as `***-**-1234`, and Medicare/MBI or other full account/insurance numbers as `****1234`. Do not mask display names, usernames, DOB, or general fields. Never log a raw SSN or full identifier to the console. If a masking utility exists, apply it only to those sensitive-identifier fields — never to names — and wire it in; never leave it as a dead, unused file.

### 9. No dead code, no schema drift, no stale framework directives

- **No dead code / no schema drift.** Any field a component reads must be defined in the data it consumes (no reading a `claimId` against records that only define `id`). Any utility, context, or masker you create must be imported and used. Keep the id field name identical across the data file and every consumer.
- **No stale framework directives.** Do not emit directives that belong to a different framework than the one in use (for example, a client-component directive in a plain Vite/CRA app); their presence signals a wrong template.

## Source-level preflight before E2E

After implementation and before the final E2E run, perform a short
source-level preflight. This is a model-guided review, not a separate
scanner or test tool. The model cannot see images — `read_file` returns
garbled bytes for PNGs — so the review reads source and Playwright's
text-based APIs, not screenshots:

1. Re-read the UI brief and confirm the chosen `new`, `preserve`, or `redesign`
   mode and product shape.
2. Confirm every planned page and meaningful state exists, and that no unplanned
   app shell, dashboard, or component catalogue was added.
3. Use Playwright to capture the accessibility tree
   (`page.accessibility.snapshot()`), computed styles
   (`page.evaluate(() => getComputedStyle(...))`), and rendered HTML
   structure (`page.content()`) for representative desktop and mobile views.
   Include the states needed to judge hierarchy and behavior, such as
   populated, empty, loading, error, open navigation, and dialog states when
   they exist. Save screenshots with `page.screenshot()` for the human
   reviewer — the model cannot see them.
4. `read_file` the frontend source and review it using the selected house
   style's preflight lens. Check content hierarchy, composition, density,
   consistency, brand fidelity, and generic-template signals from the HTML
   structure and CSS, not from screenshots. Treat these as contextual
   judgments, not count-based failures.
5. Fix material issues in the source, rerender affected views, then run the
   complete Playwright E2E journeys. Reuse Playwright traces as evidence; do
   not build a second visual-preflight tool.

Source-only interface conventions that cannot be inferred reliably from the
rendered browser are reviewed through the testing skill's
`web-interface-guidelines` reference. Do not duplicate its findings as
Playwright failures.

## Remember

This foundation guarantees the UI is correct, accessible, and structurally sound — not that it is *designed*. {"success":true,"tool_name":"fetch_skill","data":{"found":true,"name":"design-minimalist","body":"# Minimalist (house style)

The visual language for UIs that feel calm, precise, and content-first. The work is done by **typography, whitespace, and alignment** — not by color, borders, boxes, or effects. The guiding instinct is *remove before you add*: every line, shadow, and color must earn its place. Apply this **on top of design-system**, which owns the accessibility, primitive, and structure contracts; this skill fills in the token *values* and the visual treatment. Never trade an accessibility contract (AA contrast, focus rings, reduced motion) for the aesthetic.

## Prime directive: derive, don't default

The failure mode of "minimalist" is **generic plain** — Inter everywhere, a pure-grey neutral ramp, and one default blue accent: the interchangeable Linear/Vercel clone. That is the model's *default*, and it makes restraint read as *empty* rather than *considered*. Minimalist is not the absence of decisions; it is **fewer decisions, each made with more care.** This skill is **opinionated about craft, variable about identity**:

- **Invariant (fixed by this style, every project):** near-monochrome discipline, the single-accent budget, hairlines-not-shadows, small radii, quick functional motion, type-and-whitespace hierarchy, the OKLCH ramp method.
- **Variable (derived per product from the brief):** the one accent hue, the neutral temperature, the actual type *families*, density, reading measure.

Read the product's concept from `project_description` / the job brief (its domain, audience, and register) and derive from *that specific product* — restraint executed with real craft, not a template.

## When NOT to choose this style

Minimalist is the right call for **internal tools, admin dashboards, enterprise software, editorial
sites, and content-first products** where the user's goal is extracting information efficiently.
It is the **wrong call** for:

- **Consumer-facing products where motivation, retention, or visual energy matter** — fitness
  apps, social platforms, gaming, lifestyle, entertainment. These products live or die on user
  engagement; a calm, restrained aesthetic works against retention goals. Use `design-modern`
  instead.
- **Products with a bold brand identity** — if the brief names a brand with personality, energy,
  or visual presence, minimalist will flatten it. Use `design-modern`.
- **Products where the PRD gives no visual direction at all** — a missing design preference is
  NOT a preference for minimalism. If the PRD is silent on visual style and the product is
  consumer-facing, do NOT default to this style. Instead, surface the choice to the human via
  `ask_human` (see the developer-workflow skill's house-style selection rule).

The single most common failure mode is a model choosing minimalist because "the PRD didn't say
otherwise." That is a classification error, not a design decision. When in doubt, ask.

## Color — a derivation procedure for a near-monochrome palette

The palette is **neutral-driven**: surfaces, text, and borders all come from the neutral scale; color is the exception, not the rule. Run these steps in order — the procedure is fixed, its output differs per product.

**0. Honor a provided brand first.** If the brief or the task's `job_description` supplies brand colors or names a design language (see design-system's *Token values: provided brand vs. derived*), use the brand color as the single accent and set the neutral temperature from it; skip step 2. Derive only when no brand is given.

**1. Read the concept.** Name the product's register in a word or two (calm-clinical, editorial-premium, technical-utilitarian, trustworthy-precise, …).

**2. Pick the ONE accent off the concept — not the cliché.** Choose a single `primary` accent from the register, and **avoid the default SaaS blue / indigo** unless the brief truly warrants it. Because the accent is the *only* color on the screen, its hue is high-impact — a considered green, teal, warm ochre, aubergine, or deep red can define the whole product where a reflex blue says nothing. `secondary` is a **muted neutral**, never a second brand hue.

**3. Build the neutral scale perceptually (OKLCH), with a whisper of temperature.** Construct the neutral ramp (50–950) in OKLCH so lightness steps are perfectly even — an uneven or dead pure-grey ramp is the generic-plain tell. Give the neutrals a *barely perceptible* temperature bias pulled from the accent (warm accent → a hair of warmth in the greys) — a whisper, NOT the visible tint that `design-modern` uses. The neutrals ARE the palette here, so this restraint-with-craft is what separates "considered" from "lifeless."

**4. Build the accent scale (50–950) in OKLCH** for its few uses: the single primary action, focus ring, active nav, key links. Ease chroma at the extremes so it never turns neon.

**5. Quiet semantic status colors.** Desaturated red / amber / green / blue — readable but muted, used as small tonal badges and inline messages, never large filled blocks.

**6. A restrained chart palette.** Prefer sequential ramps of the accent plus one or two quiet categorical neutrals at matched low chroma; charts stay calm and legible — never rainbow, never saturated.

**Both themes first-class.** Dark mode is a **true neutral dark** (e.g. neutral-950 background, neutral-900 surface) — the whisper of temperature from step 3 aside, it is not a tinted dark like `design-modern`. No gradients.

Illustrative role values (accent hue derived per product; tune per brand):

```
light:  background #ffffff  surface #ffffff  border #e5e7eb  foreground #111827  muted #6b7280  ring <primary-500>
dark:   background #0a0a0a  surface #141414  border #262626  foreground #f5f5f5  muted #a3a3a3  ring <primary-400>
```

**Alpha-capable color tokens (if you reach for a `/opacity` modifier).** Even in this flat palette, any CSS-variable color token consumed with a Tailwind `/opacity` modifier (e.g. a faint `bg-surface/60` hover tint, `border-border/50`) MUST be defined alpha-capable — `surface: 'rgb(var(--color-surface) / <alpha-value>)'` with `--color-surface` as space-separated RGB channels (`--color-surface: 255 255 255`), OR relative-color `rgb(from var(--color-surface) r g b / <alpha-value>)` (keeps hex vars). A bare opaque `surface: 'var(--color-surface)'` CANNOT take a `/opacity` modifier: Tailwind errors `the bg-surface/60 class does not exist` and the CSS build crashes (the `@apply` form hard-crashes; JIT `.tsx` usages silently render fully opaque).

## Banned defaults (do not ship these)

- A **default blue / indigo** accent unless the brief warrants it — the single most common generic tell.
- **Inter (or the system stack) chosen by reflex for everything** — that is the absence of a type decision, not minimalism.
- A **dead, pure-grey neutral ramp** with uneven steps (build it in OKLCH; give it a whisper of temperature).
- **Shadows on default cards** (minimalist separates with a hairline), **pill-everything / large radii** (that is `design-modern`), gradients, glows, gradient borders.
- **Zebra-striped tables by default**, spinners-everywhere, and any decorative / looping / parallax motion.
- **Rainbow / saturated charts** and **emoji as icons**.

## Signature move: hierarchy without decoration, one accent as a budget

The recognizable discipline: **type and whitespace carry the entire hierarchy — not color, boxes, or rules — and the single accent is a *budget* (under ~10% of any screen) spent on the one primary action per view.** If a screen looks busy or a second color creeps in, *remove* — don't decorate. Separation is a hairline; emphasis is weight and space. This restraint, executed with the craft above, is the whole point of view.

## Content-first / admin surface craft (the quality floor)

This is the craft standard for the surfaces minimalist is chosen for — admin dashboards, data-dense tables, content-first / editorial pages, and internal tool forms. Copy the *discipline*, not a specific product.

- **Admin dashboard.** Flat KPI cards (hairline border, no shadow, tabular figures, muted trend deltas in `foreground-muted`); quiet SVG charts using the **restrained sequential accent ramp** from step 6 — never rainbow or saturated; a recent-activity feed with muted timestamps and hairline row dividers. No gradient stat cards, no glow on KPIs, no filled-color trend arrows. The dashboard's job is legibility at a glance, not visual excitement.
- **Data-dense tables.** Quiet header (muted uppercase or medium-weight labels, `scope="col"` + `aria-sort` per the foundation), hairline row dividers, generous cell padding, tabular figures so columns align. Row actions are ghost buttons (text + hairline), not filled pills. Sticky header on vertical scroll with a hairline bottom border. Loading state is skeleton rows matching the real row height; the three empty states (no-data, filtered-empty, error-with-retry) stay calm — a thin icon, one line, one action — never a large illustrated empty state. No zebra-striping unless density genuinely demands it.
- **Content-first / editorial pages.** Reading measure capped (~60–75ch per the type section), type hierarchy doing all the work: large heading, muted section labels, body at comfortable line-height. Section labels are small muted text (`foreground-muted`, medium weight, optional uppercase tracking), not colored eyebrows. No decorative elements, no pull-quote accent bars, no background tints behind sections — whitespace and weight are the structure. Generous section gaps (64–96px).
- **Forms and step wizards.** The step indicator is a hairline progress bar with step labels in muted text; the current step gets the single accent (a small dot or a one-pixel bar segment), completed steps are muted, future steps are faint — no flashy filled circles or gradient progress bars. Per-field inline validation errors sit below the input in `foreground-muted` with a quiet `error` color on the message; the invalid input gets a hairline `error` border, not a filled red background. Submit is the one accent button; cancel/reset is a ghost. Success is an inline confirmation line + a toast, not a full-page success screen.
- **Landing page (when the product needs one).** Type-led: a large heading in the display family, one short subheading in `foreground-muted`, one accent CTA, and whitespace as the feature — no gradient hero, no photo wallpaper (unless the product genuinely demands imagery), no overlapping search card (that is the `design-modern` consumer move). Section structure with muted labels and generous gaps. If the product has a primary filter or search, it sits inline below the heading as a clean hairline-bordered input, not as an elevated card on a gradient.

## Typography — the hierarchy engine (strategy fixed, families derived)

- **Strategy is fixed; families are chosen per product.** Use a **strong modular scale** (≈1.25 ratio) and let **size + weight** create hierarchy — not color, boxes, or rules. Pick the actual text family from the product's register (a clean grotesque for technical/precise; a warm humanist or a refined serif for editorial/premium) plus an optional **mono** for numerics, IDs, and code so columns align — do NOT default to Inter-for-everything without a decision.
- **Few weights:** regular (400), medium (500), semibold (600). Avoid heavy/black weights.
- **Generous line-height:** ~1.5–1.6 for body, tighter (~1.2) for large headings; slightly negative letter-spacing on big headings only.
- Cap reading measure (~60–75ch) for long text; use **tabular numerics** for any aligned figures, IDs, and tables.

## Spacing & rhythm — whitespace is the feature

- 4px base, 8px rhythm. Be **generous**: large section gaps (64–96px), airy card and control padding, comfortable line spacing.
- Constrain content to a readable max-width (~640–1100px depending on density) centered in the shell.
- Align everything to a single grid; consistent gutters. Empty space is intentional, not "unfinished."

## Elevation & shape — flat

- **Hairline borders over shadows.** Default cards have a border and **no shadow**. Reserve a single subtle shadow token for true overlays (menus, modals, popovers).
- **Small, consistent radius** (6–8px) on cards, inputs, buttons. No pill-shaped everything; no gradient borders, no glows.

## Motion — subtle and quick

- Functional only: hover, focus, enter/leave. **120–180ms, ease-out.** No decorative, looping, or parallax motion. Honor `prefers-reduced-motion` (collapse to instant).

## Icons

- Thin **1.5px stroke**, **outline only**, monochrome via `currentColor` — never multicolor or filled-color. One consistent set, optically aligned to text.

## Component styling (over design-system primitives)

- **Button:** `primary` = solid accent for the single main action; everything else is a neutral/ghost (text + hairline) variant. Hover = a subtle background tint, **not** a lift or heavy shadow. Focus-visible ring with offset, understated but clearly present.
- **Card:** border + generous padding, flat; hover (if interactive) = a faint background or border shift only.
- **Header:** flat, hairline bottom border, no glass / `backdrop-blur`, no shadow. Text-led nav items; the active section is weight + a subtle background, not a colored pill. A theme toggle sits as a quiet icon button in the corner.
- **StatusBadge:** low-saturation tonal (neutral or quiet semantic), small.
- **Input/Select:** hairline border, clean focus ring, clear label; no inner shadows.
- **Nav:** text-led; active item shown by weight and a subtle background, not a bold pill.
- **DataTable:** quiet header (muted uppercase or medium-weight labels), hairline row dividers, tabular figures, plenty of cell padding; no zebra-striping unless density genuinely demands it.
- **Dashboard:** flat KPI cards (hairline border, no shadow, tabular figures, muted trend deltas); quiet SVG charts using the restrained sequential accent ramp — never rainbow or saturated; activity feed with muted timestamps and hairline dividers. No gradient stat cards, no glow, no filled-color trend arrows.

Express variants as a lookup map (per the foundation), in restrained tokens:

```tsx
const variants = {
  primary:   "bg-primary-600 text-white hover:bg-primary-700",
  secondary: "border border-border text-foreground hover:bg-surface-raised",
  ghost:     "text-foreground hover:bg-surface-raised",
};
// usage: className={variants[variant]}
```

## Craft details (the difference between plain and refined)

- Numbers align (tabular figures); optical alignment on icons-next-to-text and centered glyphs.
- Every state is considered: empty (a thin-stroke icon + one line + at most one action), loading (neutral skeletons matching the real layout, not spinners-everywhere), error (a clear cause + retry).
- The accent budget holds — if a second color or a shadow appears, it earns its place or it is removed.
- Text meets AA on its intended `background`/`surface` role tokens in every
  supported theme.

## Visual-preflight lens

Use this lens after implementation by reviewing the rendered HTML structure
(`page.content()`), accessibility tree (`page.accessibility.snapshot()`), and
computed styles (`page.evaluate(() => getComputedStyle(...))`) via Playwright's
text-based APIs — not screenshots. The model cannot see images; screenshots are
saved with `page.screenshot()` for the human reviewer only. This lens guides
judgment; it is not a mechanical pass/fail checklist.

- The reading order and primary action are clear from the accessibility tree
  without relying on decoration.
- Whitespace groups related content and separates tasks; check computed spacing
  values — it is not empty space left by missing content or an unnecessarily
  sparse desktop layout.
- Cards, borders, pills, badges, and muted labels appear only where they clarify
  structure or status. Remove nested containers and repeated chrome.
- Repeated pages share alignment and density, while their composition follows the
  content instead of cloning one section template everywhere.
- Desktop and mobile preserve the same hierarchy, useful density, and readable
  measure — verify via computed styles and the accessibility tree in both
  viewports.
- In `preserve` mode, extensions use the existing product's tokens and component
  grammar, even when this skill would otherwise choose a different accent or
  spacing rhythm.
- If the HTML structure and token usage read as an interchangeable admin
  template, strengthen the product-specific information hierarchy rather than
  adding visual effects.

## Concrete reference specifics (from the taste-skill minimalist protocol)

The derivation procedures above are the primary method. These concrete
specifics are reference values for when the derivation lands on a warm
monochrome editorial register — use them as defaults when the brief gives
no specific font or pastel direction, not as overrides for a brand decision.

### Font families (concrete picks per role)

- **Primary sans (body, UI, buttons):** `SF Pro Display`, `Geist Sans`,
  `Helvetica Neue`, `Switzer` — clean, geometric, or system-native with
  character. Do NOT default to Inter, Roboto, or Open Sans.
- **Editorial serif (hero headings, quotes):** `Lyon Text`, `Newsreader`,
  `Playfair Display`, `Instrument Serif` — tight tracking
  (`letter-spacing: -0.02em` to `-0.04em`), tight line-height (`1.1`).
- **Monospace (code, keystrokes, metadata):** `Geist Mono`, `SF Mono`,
  `JetBrains Mono`.

### Muted pastel accent hex values (for tags, inline code, icon backgrounds)

These are the desaturated pastel tokens for small tonal badges — not the
primary accent (which is derived per product in the color section above).

- Pale Red: `#FDEBEC` (text: `#9F2F2D`)
- Pale Blue: `#E1F3FE` (text: `#1F6C9F`)
- Pale Green: `#EDF3EC` (text: `#346538`)
- Pale Yellow: `#FBF3DB` (text: `#956400`)

### Component specifics (concrete patterns)

- **Bento box feature grids:** asymmetrical CSS Grid; cards with exactly
  `border: 1px solid #EAEAEA`; border-radius 8px or 12px max; internal
  padding 24px to 40px.
- **Primary CTA:** solid `#111111` background, `#FFFFFF` text; slight
  border-radius (4px to 6px); no box-shadow; hover = subtle color shift to
  `#333333` or `scale(0.98)`.
- **Tags / status badges:** pill-shaped (`border-radius: 9999px`), very
  small typography (`text-xs`), uppercase with wide tracking
  (`letter-spacing: 0.05em`); background uses the muted pastels above.
- **Accordions (FAQ):** strip all container boxes; separate items with
  `border-bottom: 1px solid #EAEAEA`; use a clean `+` / `-` icon for toggle.
- **Keystroke micro-UIs:** render shortcuts as physical keys using `<kbd>`
  tags: `border: 1px solid #EAEAEA`, `border-radius: 4px`,
  `background: #F7F6F3`, monospace font.
- **Faux-OS window chrome:** when mocking up software, wrap it in a
  minimalist container with a white top bar containing three small light
  gray circles (replicating macOS window controls).

### Staggered reveal animation formula

For grid items and lists entering the viewport:

```css
animation-delay: calc(var(--index) * 80ms);
```

Pair with `translateY(12px)` + `opacity: 0` resolving over `600ms` with
`cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)`. Use `IntersectionObserver`, never
`window.addEventListener('scroll')`.

### Background ambient motion (optional, for hero depth)

A single, very slow-moving radial gradient blob (`animation-duration: 20s+`,
`opacity: 0.02-0.04`) drifting behind hero sections. Must be on a
`position: fixed; pointer-events: none` layer — never on scrolling
containers (continuous GPU repaints destroy mobile FPS).

## North star

Think reference docs, reading-grade clarity, and quiet admin tools: confident whitespace, one carefully-chosen accent, type doing the heavy lifting. Restraint that reads as *deliberate*, never as unfinished. If it could be any admin template, it isn't done.","reference_name":null,"reference_body":null,"suggestions":[],"summary":"Fetched skill design-minimalist"},"error":null,"decided_action":null,"persona_delta":null}

{"success":true,"tool_name":"fetch_skill","data":{"found":true,"name":"testing","body":"# Testing

Test rules across all app types. Testing is **deep, not shallow** — every
function, every endpoint, every user-facing feature gets thorough coverage
with happy paths AND negative cases. The app type determines which test
layers are required; every layer applies to every app type that has the
surface area for it.

## When this applies

Every project — static, backend-only, or fullstack. Pair with the relevant
stack skill for app/runtime conventions.

## Workflow

Follow these steps in order. Each step maps to a section below.

1. **Discover the stack** — read the project's dependency manifest, find
   the test runner, find where tests live. (See "Discover the stack
   first" under Layer 1.)
2. **Determine required test layers** — check the app-type table. A
   backend requires API tests; a frontend requires E2E; fullstack
   requires both; multi-feature with a backend requires integration.
3. **Set up test config and dependencies** — add the test runner,
   framework, and assertion library to the project's manifest. (See
   "Config and dependencies" under Layer 1.)
4. **Write unit/component tests per slice** — every service method, every
   component, every pure function gets happy-path AND negative tests.
   Write these alongside each feature slice during the implementing
   loop, not at the end. (See Layer 1.)
5. **Write API tests per slice** — every endpoint gets tested against
   the real database, in-process. (See Layer 2.)
6. **Write E2E spec files per slice** — each feature slice writes its
   own `e2e/<feature>.spec.ts` as a deliverable during the implementing
   loop. The spec is written now; it is RUN later against live servers.
   (See Layer 3.)
7. **Run the slice's tests and verify** — unit AND API tests pass before
   committing the slice. No commit on failed tests.
8. **After all slices: run the test-critic loop** — the critic loop
   reviews unit/API test coverage and quality. E2E and integration tests
   are NOT run until the critic loop is complete (passes with score
   >= 0.95 or 5 rounds exhausted). (See `fetch_skill("testing",
   reference="test-critic")`.)
9. **After all slices: write integration tests** — cross-feature data
   flows, shared state consistency, error propagation. (See Layer 2.5.)
10. **After all slices: run E2E tests** — start real servers, run
    Playwright against the live app, assert on content, capture console
    errors. The spec files were written per-slice; this step RUNS them.
    (See Layer 3 + Playwright sandbox setup.)
11. **Run the verification gate** — self-check every checkbox before
    declaring the testing phase done. (See "Verification gate" at the
    end.)

| App type | Unit/component | API tests | Integration | E2E |

| **Static (frontend-only)** | Yes — components, utils, routing | No (no backend) | If multi-feature | Yes — Playwright against the live static site |
| **Backend-only** | Yes — services, models, logic | Yes — every endpoint | If multi-feature | No (no frontend) |
| **Fullstack** | Yes — both tiers | Yes — every endpoint | If multi-slice | Yes — full user journeys |
| **Unknown / CLI** | Yes — logic, utils | If has HTTP surface | If multi-feature | If has user-facing UI |

The governance hook enforces this: backend markers in `tech_stack` require

## Layer 1 — Unit / component tests

### Discover the stack first (mandatory before writing any test)

The testing principles below are universal; the commands and tooling are
not. Before writing the first test, discover how **this** project tests
and use its commands for every test run:

- **Read the dependency manifest** to identify the exact stack and
  versions: `package.json` (Node/React/Vue/Angular/Svelte),
  `requirements.txt` / `pyproject.toml` (Python/Django/Flask/FastAPI),
  `pom.xml` / `build.gradle` (Java/Spring), `go.mod` (Go),
  `*.csproj` (.NET/ASP.NET), `Cargo.toml` (Rust), `Gemfile` (Ruby/Rails).
- **Find the test runner** the project uses — check the manifest for
  test scripts, check for a `pytest.ini`/`vitest.config.ts`/`jest.config.js`,
  check the README or CI workflow for the actual test command.
- **Find where tests live** — `__tests__/`, `tests/`, `src/**/*.test.ts`,
  `src/test/java/`, `tests/<App>.Tests/` — and follow the existing
  naming convention.
- **Never assume a default** like `npm test`. A Gradle, pytest, or
  `dotnet test` project has its own equivalent. Using the wrong runner
  produces zero test results that look like a pass.

State what you found explicitly before writing tests. If the project
has no test setup yet, choose the runner that matches the detected
stack (see "Config and dependencies" below) and set it up.

### Config and dependencies

Choose the test configuration and dependencies that match the detected stack:

- **Vite + React (TS/JS):** add a vitest config; add `vitest`,
  `@testing-library/react`, `@testing-library/jest-dom`,
  `@testing-library/user-event` to devDependencies. See

- **Next.js (TS/JS):** use either jest or vitest. For jest: add a jest
  config; add `jest`, `@testing-library/react`, `@testing-library/jest-dom`,

  config; add `vitest`, `@testing-library/react`, `@testing-library/jest-dom`,
  `@testing-library/user-event` to devDependencies. Vitest is simpler to
  configure with Next.js (no jsdom environment setup beyond the config).
  Pick one and use it consistently. See
  `fetch_skill("testing", reference="react-testing")` for patterns.
- **Node + Express (TS/JS):** add `vitest` (or `jest`) plus `supertest` and

  `fetch_skill("testing", reference="node-express-testing")` for

- **Python + FastAPI:** add `pytest`, `httpx`, `pytest-asyncio` to the

  `fetch_skill("testing", reference="python-fastapi-testing")` for

- **Java + Spring Boot:** `spring-boot-starter-test` (test scope)
  includes JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, and MockMvc. Add

  `@WebMvcTest`/MockMvc, `@DataJpaTest`, `@SpringBootTest` patterns,
  and concrete service-method test examples.
- **Go:** use the built-in `testing` package; add `testify` only if

- **.NET / ASP.NET Core:** add a separate `tests/<App>.Tests` project
  with `xunit`, `Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk`, and
  `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing`. See
  `fetch_skill("testing", reference="dotnet-testing")` for the full

  (`django.test`, `pytest` + Flask, `go test`, Jasmine/Vitest, `rails
  test`, `phpunit`, etc.) with a real file-backed database per test.
  The per-stack references above are available as patterns to adapt —
  the testing principles (service-method coverage, branch coverage,
  state-transition verification, negative cases) apply regardless of
  framework. When adapting, map the concepts: "service method" = the
  layer that holds business logic in that framework; "API test" = the
  framework's HTTP test client against a real app instance; "component
  test" = the framework's component/render testing utility.

### Entry point

Wire up the test entry point so tests are runnable the standard way:

- `package.json` must have a `"test"` script (e.g. `"vitest run"` or `"jest"`).
- Python: include pytest configuration via `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` in
  `pyproject.toml` or a `pytest.ini`.
- Go: tests run with `go test ./...`; include that in the Makefile.
- .NET: tests run with `dotnet test tests/<App>.Tests` (or
  `$HOME/.dotnet/dotnet test` if `dotnet` is not on PATH in the sandbox).

### File layout and naming

Place test files where the toolchain expects them — alongside source
(`ComponentName.test.tsx` next to `ComponentName.tsx`), in `__tests__/`
(JS/TS), or in `tests/` (Python) — and name them by the per-stack
convention:

- TypeScript/JavaScript: `ComponentName.test.tsx`, `service.test.ts`
- Python: `test_module.py` (`test_` prefix)
- Go: `module_test.go` (`_test` suffix)
- .NET: `<Feature>Tests.cs`, `<Feature>ApiTests.cs` in
  `tests/<App>.Tests/` (e.g. `ProceduralTests.cs`, `ProceduralApiTests.cs`)

Plan at least one test file per major feature module. Skip config files,
type-only files, and constants — there's no behavior to cover there.

### What unit/component tests cover

- Individual component rendering, prop handling, conditional rendering,
  user-event interactions.
- Individual API endpoint logic: status codes, validation, error handling,
  edge cases — via `supertest` (Express) or `httpx.AsyncClient` (FastAPI)
  against the app in-process, with external services mocked.
- Business logic: pure functions, service methods, state transitions.
- Don't test third-party libraries; cover only your own code.
- Avoid snapshot tests unless explicitly requested — they're brittle.

### Writing tests

Use the idiomatic approach for each stack:

- **React components:** `@testing-library/react` with `render()` plus
  `screen` queries (`getByRole`, `getByText`, `findByText` for async). Test
  user-visible behavior, never internal state. See
  `fetch_skill("testing", reference="react-testing")` for component,
  hook, and service/API client test examples.
- **API routes / Express handlers:** `supertest` to exercise the real HTTP
  request/response cycle and assert on status codes and bodies. See
  `fetch_skill("testing", reference="node-express-testing")` for
  service-method test examples and supertest patterns.
- **Python FastAPI:** `httpx.AsyncClient` against the app, marking async
  tests with `pytest.mark.asyncio`. See
  `fetch_skill("testing", reference="python-fastapi-testing")` for
  fixtures, `dependency_overrides`, and service-function test examples.
- **Java Spring Boot:** JUnit 5 with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`
  for service tests, `@WebMvcTest` + MockMvc for controller tests,
  `@DataJpaTest` for repository tests, AssertJ for assertions. See
  `fetch_skill("testing", reference="java-springboot-testing")` for
  concrete patterns.
- **Go:** `testing.T` with table-driven tests; `testify/assert` for cleaner
  assertions when available.
- **.NET / ASP.NET Core:** xUnit `[Fact]` and `[Theory]`+`[InlineData]`
  for unit tests; `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` with
  `PostAsJsonAsync`/`ReadFromJsonAsync` for API tests. See
  `fetch_skill("testing", reference="dotnet-testing")` for concrete
  service-method test examples and the `WebApplicationFactory` setup.

Give every test file the same baseline: import the module under test, at
least one happy-path test and at least one negative/edge-case test,
descriptive names that state what is tested and the expected outcome.

### Depth — happy AND negative cases

Every function, method, and endpoint must have happy-path AND negative
tests. See `fetch_skill("testing", reference="negative-cases")` for the
full list of negative test case categories (invalid types, missing fields,
boundary values, unauthorized access, non-existent resources, duplicates,
security boundaries, large payloads) and depth rules.

### Mocking boundary

- **Unit and component tests:** mock external service dependencies (network
  calls to third-party APIs, filesystem); real network requests make tests
  flaky and slow. **Do NOT mock the application's own database** — even in
  unit tests, use the real database specified in the design documents with
  a test schema/database. The database is the app's core state; mocking it
  hides the exact bugs tests exist to catch.
- **API tests:** never mock the database — run against the real database
  engine specified in the PRD/HLD/LLD (see Layer 2 above).
- **E2E tests:** do NOT mock anything — test against the real running app
  with the real database. See Layer 3 below.
- For async code, await assertions, use `waitFor()` for React state
  changes — otherwise you assert before the update lands.

## Layer 2 — API tests (any app with a backend)

API tests sit between unit tests and E2E: they exercise the real backend
HTTP surface against the real database specified in the design documents,
without the frontend. Required for **any app with a backend** —
backend-only OR fullstack.

- **If the app uses a database, API tests MUST run against the real
  database specified in the PRD/HLD/LLD — never mocked, never substituted
  with an in-memory stand-in.** This is the layer where database behavior
  is verified: schema constraints, foreign keys, cascading deletes, unique
  violations, transaction rollback, query correctness, and
  database-specific features (JSONB, enums, partial indexes, etc.).
  Mocking the database or swapping it for SQLite in-memory means you are
  testing your mocks, not your app — and hides bugs that only surface
  against the real engine the app will ship with.
  Install the real database in the sandbox (e.g.
  `sudo apt-get install -y postgresql` for PostgreSQL,
  `sudo apt-get install -y mongodb` for MongoDB) and configure a test
  database instance. The only exception is when the upstream design
  documents **explicitly** specify an in-memory or embedded database
  (e.g. SQLite is the production database) — in that case test against
  exactly what the design calls for, still never a mock.
- Run **before** E2E — they catch backend contract bugs early.
- Use the same tooling as unit tests (`httpx.AsyncClient` for FastAPI,
  `supertest` for Express) but against a real app instance with a real or
  in-memory database, not mocked.
- Cover every endpoint: status codes, request/response shapes, auth
  boundaries, error cases — both happy AND negative paths.
- Tenant isolation and workspace-scoped authorization get their own tests —
  these are security-critical and E2E won't catch every permutation.

## Layer 2.5 — Cross-feature integration tests (multi-feature apps with a backend)

When the app has more than one feature slice AND a backend, per-feature API
tests are necessary but NOT sufficient. Write integration tests that
exercise the **full cross-feature data flows** — not just one chained call,
but every path where features interact.

### What integration tests cover

- Data flows correctly across feature boundaries — a record created by one
  router is usable by another, with consistent identity and ownership.
- Shared state (auth, user identity, ownership) is consistent across
  features.
- The multi-step user journeys from the upstream design are exercised.
- Error propagation across features — when one feature's upstream
  dependency fails, the downstream feature handles it gracefully (no silent
  data loss, no orphaned records, correct error status).

### Coverage scope — DEEP

- Test **every cross-feature data flow**, not just one. If feature A creates
  data that feature B reads, feature C modifies, and feature D displays —
  write a test for each crossing, plus one that chains all four.
- Test both the **happy path** AND the **error path** (upstream data
  missing, invalid, or belongs to a different user).
- Test **shared state consistency**: after a sequence of cross-feature
  operations, verify the database state — no orphaned records, no stale
  references, no ownership leaks.
- At least one integration test that chains **three or more**
  routers/services in a single flow.
- Follow the multi-step user journeys from the upstream design when they
  exist; when they do not, derive the most natural cross-feature flows.

A frontend-only multi-page app does NOT need backend integration tests —
its cross-feature concerns are covered by E2E.

## Layer 3 — E2E tests (any app with a user-facing frontend)

E2E tests are **required** for any app with a user-facing frontend —
fullstack OR static/frontend-only. A green build or green unit tests are
not sufficient. The run is incomplete without E2E results in
`test_report.yaml`.

### What E2E covers

- The frontend renders and (for fullstack) the BFF proxies to the backend
  correctly.
- API contracts between frontend and backend are compatible across the real
  HTTP boundary (fullstack only).
- Auth/session flows work across the stack (fullstack only).
- Real user journeys complete end-to-end: the things a user would actually
  do in the running application.
- **Response content is correct** — not just "the page loaded" but the
  actual data is rendered. Assert on content that can only come from the
  backend (fullstack) or the app's data layer (static), not hardcoded
  strings.
- **Console errors are captured** — a page that renders but throws JS
  errors is broken. Use `page.on('console')` and `page.on('pageerror')` to
  capture and fail on browser-side errors.

### What E2E does NOT cover

- Individual component rendering in isolation — unit tests own this.
- Individual API endpoint logic — API tests own this.
- Edge cases in business logic — unit tests own this.

E2E is for the **wiring and the journey**, not the logic.

### Source-level web-interface review

After UI implementation and before visual preflight, review the changed frontend
source using `fetch_skill("testing", reference="web-interface-guidelines")`.
Apply only rules relevant to the product and stack. Fix material correctness,
accessibility, navigation, interaction, rendering, or performance findings before
the final browser run.

This review owns implementation facts that Playwright cannot infer reliably, such
as semantic element choice, blocked paste, `transition: all`, unnecessary
JavaScript layout measurement, shareable state kept only in component memory,
font-loading strategy, and avoidable main-thread work. Report findings with a
file and line when possible.

Do not use source review to judge visual personality, and do not duplicate checks
that Playwright can prove directly. If a rule has both a source and runtime aspect,
review the implementation once and let Playwright own the behavioral assertion.

### Source-level preflight before the final E2E run

For user-facing UIs, use Playwright once to support both design review and runtime
verification. Before the final E2E run, capture the accessibility tree
(`page.accessibility.snapshot()`), computed styles
(`page.evaluate(() => getComputedStyle(...))`), and rendered HTML structure
(`page.content()`) for representative desktop and mobile pages, including
meaningful states such as empty, loading, error, open navigation, and dialogs
when those states exist. `read_file` the frontend source and review it using
`design-system` and the selected house style for hierarchy, composition,
density, and generic-template signals. Save screenshots with
`page.screenshot()` for the human reviewer — the model cannot see images;
`read_file` returns garbled bytes for PNGs. Fix material issues in the source
and rerender affected views.

Keep the ownership boundary clear:

- The design skills and model judge hierarchy, composition, density, brand or
  existing-system fidelity, and whether the result feels generic — from the
  HTML structure, CSS, and Playwright's accessibility tree, not from
  screenshots.
- Playwright asserts observable behavior: journeys, responsive interactions,
  accessible names, content, network behavior, and browser errors. Screenshots
  are saved for the human reviewer; traces provide text-based evidence the model
  can read.
- Do not create a separate visual-preflight scanner, duplicate the Playwright
  suite, or turn subjective preferences into brittle numeric assertions.

The final E2E run still executes the complete user journeys after source-level
fixes.

## Test writing principles (summary)

Four principles guide how tests should be written. Fetch
`fetch_skill("testing", reference="test-principles")` for the full
explanation, examples, and the Prove-It Pattern for bug fixes.

- **DAMP over DRY** — tests read like specifications; prefer duplication
  over abstraction; shared setup is for infrastructure, not behavior.
- **The Beyonce Rule** — if you liked it, you should have put a test on
  it. Refactoring without tests is gambling.
- **Test state, not interactions** — assert on outcomes, not mock call
  counts. Tests that survive refactoring verify state.
- **Prefer real implementations over mocks** — Real > Fake > Stub >
  Mock. Never mock the app's own database.

## Common rationalizations

| Rationalization | Reality |
|---|---|
| "I wrote tests that pass" | Tests that pass without exercising service logic are not tests — they're compiler checks. A `[Fact]` that asserts a DTO getter returns a default value proves nothing about the application. |
| "This method is too simple to test" | Simple methods get complicated. The test documents the expected behavior and catches regressions when the method changes. The Beyonce Rule: if you liked it, you should have put a test on it. |
| "The test is DRY — I extracted the shared setup" | Over-DRY tests hide what they verify. DAMP over DRY: each test should read like a specification, independently understandable without tracing through helpers. |
| "I'll add tests after the code works" | Tests written after the fact test the implementation you wrote, not the behavior the spec requires. You rationalize the test to match the code. |
| "Unit tests pass — testing is done" | Unit tests are one layer. API tests, integration tests, and E2E are also required per the app-type table. "Unit tests pass" is not "testing is done." |
| "I tested it manually" | Manual testing doesn't persist. Tomorrow's change breaks it with no way to know. |
| "Mocking the database makes tests faster" | Mocking the database hides the exact bugs tests exist to catch — schema constraints, foreign keys, cascading deletes, transaction behavior. Use a real file-backed database. |
| "E2E is optional for this app" | E2E is required for any app with a user-facing frontend. A green build is not sufficient. The run is incomplete without E2E results in `test_report.yaml`. |
| "Negative cases are implied by the happy path" | They are not. Missing fields, invalid types, unauthorized access, non-existent resources, and duplicates each need their own test. See `fetch_skill("testing", reference="negative-cases")`. |
| "I don't need to discover the stack — I know how to test X" | Training data goes stale. Frameworks change their test runners, config format, and conventions. Read the project's manifest and existing tests first. |
| "All tests pass" (but no tests were actually run) | If the test command produced zero test results, that is not a pass — it's a no-op. Verify the runner executed actual test cases. |

## Red flags

- Tests that pass on the first run before the code under test exists — they're not testing what you think
- "All tests pass" but the test command output shows zero tests collected or zero assertions
- Bug fixes without a reproduction test that fails before the fix
- Tests that only assert on DTO getters, setters, or default constructor values — not service logic
- Tests that mock the application's own database
- Skipping tests (`xit`, `@pytest.mark.skip`, `@Disabled`) to make the suite pass
- Test names that don't describe the behavior being verified (`test1`, `testWorks`, `testHandler`)
- Reaching for a default test command (`npm test`) without checking what this project actually uses
- No negative/edge-case tests — only happy paths
- E2E that only checks "page loaded" without asserting on response content
- E2E that passes with the backend offline (fullstack) — the frontend is self-contained, not testing the real HTTP boundary
- Console errors during E2E that are ignored instead of failing the test
- Running the same test command twice in a row without any intervening code change — re-running unchanged code adds no confidence

## Verification gate

Before declaring the testing phase complete, verify each item. The
governance hooks enforce some of these after `complete_task` — this
gate makes the model self-check first.

- [ ] Stack and test runner discovered from the project's dependency manifest — not assumed
- [ ] Every service method has at least one happy-path test AND one negative/edge-case test
- [ ] No test file contains only DTO getter/setter assertions — service logic is exercised
- [ ] Unit tests actually ran — the test command output shows test cases collected and assertions made (not zero results)
- [ ] API tests ran against the real database specified in the design (never mocked) — for any app with a backend
- [ ] Integration tests ran for every cross-feature data flow — for multi-feature apps with a backend
- [ ] E2E tests ran against the live app with real servers — for any app with a user-facing frontend
- [ ] E2E asserts on response content, not just page load
- [ ] E2E captures and fails on browser console errors
- [ ] No tests were skipped or disabled to make the suite pass
- [ ] `test_report.yaml` lists every test layer with its command and result
